business_problem: Manual surveys did not provide an efficient way to track habitat changes across England, limiting how current habitat data could support planning and land-use decisions.
solution_summary: Natural England's Living England project combines satellite imagery with targeted field-survey evidence and applies machine learning to build a detailed map of the current extent of habitats across England. The approach replaces reliance on manual surveys alone and is intended to keep habitat information more current and consistent at national scale. The resulting map is used as decision support for planning and land-use decisions, helping accelerate proposals while supporting better protection of nature. The source describes imagery and survey information as inputs, machine-learning mapping as processing, and the map as the output consumed by decision-makers; it does not identify a named data store, software platform, vendor, deployment design, or integration with planning systems, so those implementation details cannot be specified.
data_flow: Satellite imagery and targeted field-survey observations are used as inputs to machine-learning analysis, which produces the Living England habitat map showing habitat extent across England; the resulting map supports planning and land-use decisions.
business_outcome: Habitat changes can be tracked more efficiently across England, providing more current data to speed planning and land-use decisions while better protecting nature.
architecture_clues: Living England habitat map covers England.

source_references.title: AI and satellites speed up planning approvals by tracking wild habitats across England
source_references.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, Government Digital Service, and Natural England

evidence_quotes: Satellite images and machine learning ... are being used by Natural England to build a detailed map of “Living England”, showing the current extent of habitats across the country.

Rather than the manual surveys of the past, changes to English habitats will now be tracked more efficiently and across the country – speeding up decisions around planning and land use while better protecting nature.
